name: Jojoba oil
good: Light and very close to the skin's own oil. Suits most skin types.
care: Very stable. Reactions are rare.

name: Sunflower seed oil
good: High in linoleic acid, which supports the skin barrier. Cheap and gentle.
care: Buy fresh and store away from heat.

name: Squalane (plant-derived)
good: Very light, non-greasy, and doesn't go rancid easily.
care: Choose olive- or sugarcane-derived.

name: Sweet almond oil
good: Softening on face and body.
care: Tree nut. Skip if anyone using it has a nut allergy.

name: Argan oil
good: Rich but absorbs well. Popular for dry skin and hair.
care: Tree nut. Skip if anyone using it has a nut allergy.

name: Rosehip seed oil
good: Light and high in linoleic acid. Popular for dull or uneven-looking skin.
care: Goes rancid fast. Refrigerate and use within about 3 months.

name: Grapeseed oil
good: Thin and quick to absorb.
care: Oxidizes fairly quickly. Store cool and dark.

name: Castor oil
good: Thick and glossy. Useful in small amounts for lip balms and cleansing oils.
care: Keep it a small part of a blend; large amounts feel sticky and can irritate.

name: Olive oil
good: Rich and inexpensive for body use.
care: Research found it can weaken the skin barrier, especially on dry or eczema-prone skin. Better for body than face.

name: Coconut oil
good: Moisturizing on body, hair, and lips.
care: Clogs pores for many people. Avoid in leave-on face products if you break out.

name: Neem oil
good: Traditional in Ayurvedic scalp and skin care.
care: Strong garlic-like smell and a known cause of allergic rashes. Dilute to about 10% in another oil for the face. It doesn't reliably treat fungal infections; a pharmacist can recommend an antifungal cream.

name: Pomegranate seed oil
good: Rich, antioxidant-heavy oil used in small amounts in face serums.
care: Oxidizes fairly quickly. Store cool and dark.

name: Prickly pear seed oil
good: A light, expensive Moroccan oil for the face.
care: Often diluted or counterfeit given the price. Buy from a seller who lists the INCI name Opuntia ficus-indica.

name: Baobab oil
good: Rich, stable West African oil for dry skin and hair.
care: Low risk. Heavier feel on oily skin.

name: Palm kernel oil (adwengo, ude aki, adin dudu)
good: Traditional Ghanaian oil for body and hair.
care: Can clog pores on the face. Better for body and hair.

name: Pumpkin seed oil
good: Popular in hair oils. Studies on hair growth used capsules taken by mouth, not oil on the scalp.
care: Dark green; can tint very light hair slightly.

name: Caprylic/capric triglyceride (MCT)
good: A light, non-greasy oil refined from coconut. Very stable and rarely irritating.
care: Low risk. Buy cosmetic grade.

name: Cyperus oil (souad oil)
good: Sold in Morocco as a hair growth inhibitor.
care: There's little good evidence that it slows hair regrowth. Patch test; it can irritate.

name: Garlic-infused oil
care: Garlic causes chemical burns on skin, and infused oil still carries some of that risk. Keep it off the face, rinse within 30 minutes, and stop at any burning.

name: Batana oil
good: Thick Honduran palm oil that became a viral hair oil.
care: Smoky smell and dark color. There's no good evidence it regrows hair; it works as a rich conditioning oil.

name: Apricot kernel oil
good: Light, silky oil for sensitive skin and face blends.
care: Low risk. Comes from a stone fruit kernel, not a tree nut, but check with your doctor if you have a severe nut allergy.

name: Hemp seed oil
good: Light, high-linoleic oil that suits oily skin.
care: Goes rancid quickly. Refrigerate.

name: Safflower oil (high linoleic)
good: Light and inexpensive.
care: Can trigger reactions in people allergic to daisies or ragweed.

name: Rice bran oil
good: Light oil popular in soaps and Asian skincare.
care: Low risk.

name: Sesame oil (untoasted)
good: Traditional in Ayurvedic massage and oil pulling.
care: Sesame is a common food allergen. Use untoasted oil for skin.

name: Macadamia oil
good: Rich but non-greasy.
care: Tree nut. It has no meaningful SPF, despite popular claims.

name: Tamanu oil
good: Thick green oil traditionally used on scars and blemishes.
care: From a tree nut, and allergic rashes have been reported. The scar evidence is thin. Patch test first.

name: Sea buckthorn oil
care: Very orange; it can tint skin and fabric. Use only a few percent in a blend.

name: Evening primrose oil
good: Light oil used in face blends.
care: Oxidizes quickly. Refrigerate.

name: Mustard oil
good: Traditional massage and hair oil in South Asia.
care: Contains allyl isothiocyanate, which is pungent and can irritate or burn sensitive skin and gums. Patch test, and keep it off the face.

name: Carrot-infused oil
good: Orange oil made by soaking dried carrot in a carrier oil.
care: Use fully dried carrot so no water gets in. Not the same as carrot seed essential oil.

name: Licorice root oil extract
good: Oil-soluble licorice, sold for brightening blends.
care: Low risk. The brightening studies used purified extracts like glabridin, which home-strength oils don't match.

name: Petroleum jelly (Vaseline)
good: The most effective occlusive there is: it seals moisture in better than any plant oil. Great on cracked heels and lips.
care: Cosmetic-grade petrolatum is highly purified and very rarely irritating. Too heavy for acne-prone faces.

name: Kokum butter
good: Hard, non-greasy butter that melts on contact. Good in balms and lotion bars.
care: Low risk. Can feel brittle; blend with softer butters.

name: Illipe butter
good: Firm butter similar to cocoa butter, without the chocolate smell.
care: Low risk.

name: Carnauba wax
good: Very hard plant wax. Use about a third as much as beeswax.
care: Melts at a high temperature; heat gently.

name: Oil-soluble aloe extract
good: Aloe infused into oil, so it can go in oil-only products without adding water.
care: Low risk. Usually soybean or sunflower oil based.

name: Avocado butter
good: Soft, rich butter for whipped butters and balms.
care: Low risk. Can feel heavy on fine hair.

name: Wheat germ oil
good: Rich oil, naturally high in vitamin E.
care: Skip it if you have a wheat allergy. Strong smell; use it as a small part of a blend.

name: Camellia (tsubaki) oil
good: Light, silky oil traditional in Japanese hair care; absorbs quickly.
care: Low risk.

name: Arnica-infused oil
good: Traditional for bruises and sore muscles on unbroken skin.
care: Never on broken skin or open wounds, and never swallowed. Skip it if you're allergic to daisies, ragweed, or chamomile.

name: Marula oil
good: Light, stable oil rich in oleic acid.
care: Low risk; it's a nut oil, so skip it with tree nut allergies.

name: Aloe butter
good: Soft butter made from aloe extract in coconut oil; no water.
care: Low risk.

name: Murumuru butter
good: Firm Amazonian butter, popular for hair and dry skin.
care: Low risk. Like any butter, it moisturizes; it doesn't treat eczema or boost collagen.

name: Tucuma butter
good: Light Amazonian butter for hair and skin.
care: Low risk.

name: Bacuri butter
good: Dark, rich butter that absorbs fast.
care: It can tint skin and fabrics brown. Patch test.

name: Mafura butter
good: Soft African butter for dry skin and hair.
care: Low risk.

name: Andiroba oil
good: Thick Amazonian oil used traditionally on skin and as an insect deterrent.
care: Very bitter smell and can irritate some people. Patch test; it treats no disease.

name: Crambe oil
good: Very stable, silky oil, a bit like jojoba.
care: Low risk.

name: Cacay (kahai) oil
good: Light, silky nut oil for face and hair.
care: A nut oil; skip it with tree nut allergies. It doesn't contain prescription-strength retinoic acid.

name: Açaí berry oil
good: Green, antioxidant-rich oil for face blends.
care: Can tint pale products green. Low risk.

name: Plum kernel oil
good: Light oil with a soft almond-marzipan scent.
care: Low risk; patch test if you react to almonds or stone fruit.

name: Mongongo (manketti) oil
good: Light African nut oil for skin and hair.
care: Its fatty acids don't make it a sunscreen.

name: Desert date (balanites) oil
good: Light African oil for dry hair and skin.
care: Low risk.

name: Mineral oil
good: Very gentle, non-allergenic, and doesn't go rancid.
care: Low risk on skin. Never swallow or inhale it.

name: Avocado oil
good: Rich and nourishing for dry skin.
care: Heavy feel. May be too rich for oily skin.

name: Beef tallow
good: Rich, occlusive balm base that seals in moisture.
care: Can clog pores on the face. Choose well-rendered, odorless tallow and keep the jar sealed, because it can go rancid.

name: Ghee (clarified butter)
good: Traditional rich balm for dry lips and skin.
care: It's a food fat that goes rancid and can smell. Make small amounts and keep it cool.

name: Shea butter
good: Rich and soothing. Softens very dry skin.
care: Comes from a nut, but refined shea rarely causes nut reactions. Ask your doctor if you have a severe nut allergy.

name: Mango butter
good: Softer and less greasy than shea.
care: Mango allergy is possible but uncommon.

name: Cocoa butter
good: Firm and rich. Good for body butters and lip balms.
care: Can clog pores on the face.

name: Beeswax
good: Thickens balms and leaves a protective layer.
care: Bee-product allergies are possible.

name: Candelilla wax
good: Plant wax. You need about half as much as beeswax.
care: Makes balms firm quickly; add slowly.

name: Distilled water
good: The clean base for any water-based product.
care: Anything containing water can grow bacteria and mold. Make it fresh or add a broad-spectrum preservative.

name: Tap water
care: Tap water carries microbes and minerals. Use distilled, or boiled water that has cooled.

name: Aloe vera gel (pure, store-bought)
good: Soothing and hydrating.
care: Check the label for alcohol and fragrance. Counts as water for spoilage.

name: Aloe gel from a fresh leaf
care: The yellow sap under the leaf skin irritates skin. Let it drain and rinse the clear gel. Spoils within days.

name: Rose or chamomile hydrosol
good: Gentle, lightly scented floral water.
care: Counts as water, so it spoils without a preservative. Refrigerate once opened.

name: Flaxseed gel
good: Slippery gel from boiled flaxseed. Popular for defining curls and taming frizz.
care: Spoils within a few days, even refrigerated. Make small batches.

name: Chia seed gel
good: Slippery, hydrating gel like flaxseed gel.
care: Spoils within a few days, even refrigerated.

name: Magnesium chloride flakes
good: Dissolved in water, it makes "magnesium oil", a salty solution that feels oily.
care: It often tingles or itches, especially on freshly shaved skin. Keep it off the face and out of eyes. There's little evidence that skin absorbs meaningful magnesium.

name: Herbal tea or decoction (mint, chamomile, neem leaf, curry leaf)
good: A gentle, fragrant liquid for masks and hair rinses.
care: Spoils like any drink. Make fresh. Mint can tingle near the eyes.

name: Brewed green tea, cooled
good: Antioxidant-rich liquid for masks and rinses.
care: Spoils like any drink. Make fresh.

name: Witch hazel
care: Most drugstore witch hazel contains about 14% alcohol, which can dry and sting. Look for alcohol-free.

name: Rice water
care: A popular toner, but it's starchy water that grows bacteria within a day or two, faster if fermented. Make it fresh and use it the same day.

name: Vegetable glycerin
good: Draws water into the skin.
care: Above about 5% it feels sticky.

name: Raw honey
good: Soothing, mildly antibacterial, and hydrating. Great in rinse-off masks.
care: Sticky. Bee-product allergies are possible.

name: Plain yogurt
good: Contains gentle lactic acid. Soothing in masks.
care: Food: use right away, never store. Skip if allergic to dairy.

name: Milk
good: Mild and soothing in masks and soaks.
care: Food: use right away, never store.

name: Mashed avocado
good: Creamy and rich for dry-skin masks.
care: Food: use right away, never store.

name: Mashed banana
good: Soft base for hydrating masks.
care: Food: use right away, never store.

name: Blended cucumber
good: Cooling and refreshing.
care: Food: use right away, never store.

name: Mashed papaya
good: Papain enzyme gives a gentle exfoliating effect in masks.
care: Food: use right away. Rinse off within 10 minutes, sooner if it tingles.

name: Mashed pineapple
care: Bromelain breaks down skin's surface quickly. Leave it on 5 minutes at most and rinse at the first sting.

name: Tomato pulp
care: The juice can sting and redden skin, especially sensitive skin. Rinse within 10 minutes. Food: use right away.

name: Coconut milk
good: Creamy and soothing in masks and hair treatments.
care: Food: use right away, never store.

name: Sour cream
good: Contains gentle lactic acid, like yogurt.
care: Food: use right away. Skip if allergic to dairy.

name: Apple juice
good: Mild fruit acids in rinse-off masks.
care: Can sting broken skin. Food: use right away.

name: Onion juice
flag: Onion juice can irritate the scalp
care: Strong smell, stings scratched skin, and can cause rashes. The hair regrowth evidence is one small study in people with alopecia areata. Patch test and rinse within 30 minutes.

name: Carrot juice
good: Adds color and beta-carotene to rinse-off products.
care: Food: spoils fast. Can tint pale skin orange in large amounts.

name: Cooked rice, mashed
good: A soft, starchy base for masks.
care: Food: use right away, never store.

name: Okra (boiled for gel)
good: Boiled okra makes a slippery, hydrating gel.
care: Spoils within days. It doesn't contain or make collagen.

name: Fresh ginger
good: Warming in foot soaks.
care: Stings broken skin and the face. Keep it in soaks and body products.

name: Beetroot, blended
care: Tints light hair, skin, nails, and towels pink. The color washes out of hair within a few shampoos. Food: use the same day.

name: Camel milk
care: Raw camel milk can carry brucellosis and other infections. Use pasteurized milk, and like any milk, use it right away.

name: Fresh lemon or lime zest
flag: Fresh zest can sun-sensitize and spoil
care: Citrus peel carries the compounds that cause sun burns and dark patches, and fresh zest adds moisture that spoils stored scrubs. Use dried peel or a phototoxicity-free citrus oil.

name: Fresh orange zest or juice
flag: Fresh orange spoils in a jar
care: Far less sun-sensitizing than lemon or lime, but fresh zest and juice add water and sugar that spoil stored scrubs. Use dried peel to make a scrub that keeps.

name: Mashed fruit (strawberry, mango)
care: Mashed fruit carries water and sugar into oil and wax, where mold grows within days. Use a lip-safe flavor oil for the scent instead.

name: Malai (fresh milk cream)
good: Rich and soothing for a few minutes as a mask or lip treatment.
care: Dairy spoils fast. Make it fresh, or keep it in the fridge for 1 to 2 days at most.

name: Raw egg white or yolk
care: Wash hands and surfaces after, keep it away from mouth and eyes, rinse off fully, and never store it.

name: Colloidal oatmeal
good: Calms itchy, dry skin. One of the best-studied gentle DIY ingredients.
care: Very low risk. Oat allergy is rare.

name: Kaolin clay
good: The gentlest clay. Suits normal to dry skin.
care: Rinse off before it dries and cracks.

name: Bentonite clay
good: Strong oil-absorbing clay for oily skin.
care: Can be very drying. Leave on 5 to 10 minutes at most.

name: Rice flour
good: Fine, soft exfoliant that's gentle enough for the face.
care: Rub lightly. Once or twice a week is plenty.

name: Arrowroot or cornstarch
good: Absorbs oil and gives balms a silky, less greasy feel.
care: Very low risk.

name: Turmeric powder
flag: Turmeric stains and can cause allergy
care: Stains skin, nails, and towels yellow and can cause allergic rashes. Use a pinch and patch test first.

name: Blue clay
good: A mid-strength clay for normal to oily skin.
care: Rinse off before it dries. Products sold as blue clay vary a lot; some are dyed.

name: Wild turmeric (kasturi manjal)
good: A different plant from cooking turmeric, traditional in South Indian masks. Stains much less.
care: Patch test first and keep it away from the eyes.

name: Fenugreek (methi) seeds or powder
care: Fenugreek is related to peanuts and chickpeas and can cause reactions in people allergic to them. Strong maple-like smell.

name: Talc
care: Loose talc irritates the lungs when inhaled, and cosmetic talc has had asbestos contamination problems. Cornstarch or kaolin do the same job.

name: Gram flour (besan)
good: Traditional South Asian face wash and mask base. Gently absorbs oil.
care: Chickpea-based, so skip it with a legume allergy. Rinse well.

name: Instant or finely ground coffee powder
good: Fine powder that colors masks without scratching like coarse grounds.
care: The claim that coffee reduces tanning or dark circles is weak. Rinse well; it can tint light towels.

name: Red lentil flour (masoor dal)
good: Traditional mild exfoliating flour in South Asian face washes.
care: Skip with a legume allergy.

name: Neem leaf powder
good: Bitter herb used in Ayurvedic face packs.
care: Can be drying, and neem allergy is possible. Patch test.

name: Sandalwood powder (chandan)
good: Cooling, fragrant powder for face packs.
care: Often cut with cheaper wood. Red sandalwood powder stains.

name: Amla (Indian gooseberry) powder
good: Traditional in hair masks and oils.
care: Mildly acidic; can sting a scratched scalp.

name: Moringa leaf powder
good: Green leaf powder for masks and hair oils.
care: Low risk; colors masks green.

name: Saffron
care: The most expensive spice, so it's commonly dyed or mixed with fillers. Stains skin yellow. A pinch is plenty.

name: Aker fassi (Moroccan lip and cheek tint)
flag: Check what's in your aker fassi
care: Traditionally poppy and pomegranate, but some sold today contain synthetic dyes. Patch test before using on lips.

name: Henna (pure, Lawsonia)
good: Traditional hair dye and skin decoration.
care: Stains orange-red for days. Pure henna is never black.

name: Ayilo clay (calabash chalk)
care: Fine as a rinse-off mask. It's also sold as a snack in West Africa, and studies have found lead and other heavy metals in some samples. Never eat it, especially during pregnancy.

name: Epsom salt
good: Classic for warm foot and bath soaks.
care: Skin absorbs very little magnesium; the warm water does the relaxing.

name: Mustard seed or powder
care: Warming in foot soaks, but it can burn. Never on the face.

name: Cayenne or chili pepper
care: Capsaicin burns skin and eyes. Small amounts in foot soaks only; wash your hands afterward.

name: Shikakai powder
good: Traditional Indian hair wash powder that lathers gently.
care: Stings badly in the eyes.

name: Aritha (reetha, soapnut) powder
good: Natural soapy hair wash.
care: Strongly irritating to eyes. Can dry the scalp with daily use.

name: Bhringraj powder
good: Ayurvedic herb in hair oils and masks.
care: Low risk. The hair growth evidence comes from animal studies.

name: Brahmi powder
good: Ayurvedic herb used in hair oils.
care: Low risk.

name: Tulsi (holy basil) leaves or powder
good: Fragrant herb in hair and face packs.
care: Low risk.

name: Ashwagandha powder
good: Added to some hair oils.
care: The evidence is for taking it by mouth, not for hair. Low risk on the scalp.

name: Powdered milk
good: Makes a soft, milky bath and helps disperse essential oils.
care: Keep it dry. Skip with a dairy allergy.

name: Honey powder
good: Dry honey for bath soaks, so the jar stays dry.
care: Clumps in humid bathrooms; keep the lid tight.

name: Spirulina powder
good: Colors bath soaks and masks green.
care: Can stain grout and tubs. It doesn't detox anything.

name: Kelp or seaweed powder
good: Sea-scented powder for bath teas and masks.
care: Smells strongly of the sea. Contains iodine; avoid with an iodine allergy.

name: Dried ginger (powder or pieces)
good: Warming feel in bath teas and foot soaks.
care: Can tingle on sensitive skin. Keep it out of face products.

name: Green tea powder or matcha
good: Antioxidant-rich powder for masks and bath teas.
care: Can tint the tub slightly green.

name: Almond powder (almond meal)
good: Soft, gentle exfoliant for face scrubs.
care: Tree nut. Skip with a nut allergy.

name: Cocoa powder
good: Color and chocolate scent in masks and scrubs.
care: Low risk. Can tint towels brown.

name: Rose petal powder
good: Color and light scent in face masks.
care: Low risk. Keep dry until use.

name: Caramel sauce
care: Mostly sugar and cream. Fine in a scrub you use right away, but it doesn't keep, and homemade caramel is dangerously hot when made.

name: Purple Brazilian clay
good: Gentle clay that adds a soft purple to mauve color to soaps and masks.
care: Rinse off before it dries. Like all clays, it absorbs oil; it doesn't remove toxins.

name: Annatto powder
good: Natural yellow-orange colorant for soaps.
care: Can stain washcloths. Allergy is uncommon but possible.

name: Manjistha (madder root) powder
good: Natural colorant that turns soap pink to deep red.
care: Low risk. It colors, it doesn't whiten skin or cure acne.

name: Sidr (jujube leaf) powder
good: Traditional mild cleansing powder for hair and skin, mixed with water into a paste.
care: Mix only what you'll use. Rinse well; it can feel drying on very dry hair.

name: Avocado seed powder
good: Dried, ground avocado pit used as a scrub and to tint masks.
care: Home-ground seed has sharp, uneven bits, so keep it gentle and off broken skin. The "detox" and anti-aging claims aren't backed by good evidence.

name: Pink clay
good: A mix of white and red clay. Gentle enough for sensitive and normal skin.
care: Rinse off before it dries.

name: Red clay
good: Iron-rich clay for normal skin.
care: Can tint pale skin and towels slightly pink. Rinse off before it dries.

name: Rhassoul (ghassoul) clay
good: Moroccan clay with a silky feel. Absorbs oil without being as drying as bentonite. Used in hammam masks and as a hair wash.
care: Rinse off after 5 to 10 minutes.

name: French green clay
good: Strongly oil-absorbing clay for oily skin.
care: Very drying. Leave on 5 to 10 minutes at most, and skip it on dry or sensitive skin.

name: Fuller's earth (multani mitti)
good: Highly absorbent clay, popular in South Asian skincare for oily skin.
care: Can be very drying. Never use it on sunburn, despite popular claims.

name: Nila powder (Moroccan blue)
flag: Nila powder stains and is often adulterated
care: Stains skin, nails, and grout blue. Much of what's sold is mixed with synthetic dyes. Buy one that lists pure Indigofera and patch test first.

name: Gotu kola (centella) powder
good: The calming herb behind many "cica" products. Gentle in rinse-off masks.
care: Allergy is rare. Dried herb powder is much weaker than the extracts in store-bought products.

name: Licorice root powder
good: Traditionally used to calm redness and even tone in masks.
care: Low risk. The brightening results in studies come from purified extracts, not kitchen powder.

name: Willow bark powder or extract
care: It contains salicin, a weak plant relative of salicylic acid that doesn't exfoliate like a BHA product. Skip it if you're allergic to aspirin.

name: Lemon or lime peel powder
care: Citrus peel holds the compounds that cause sun-triggered burns and dark patches. Never in leave-on products; rinse-off only, and stay out of the sun for 12 hours.

name: Orange peel powder
good: A popular brightening mask ingredient with a mild texture.
care: Far less sun-sensitizing than lemon or lime peel, but can irritate. Rinse-off only.

name: Hyaluronic acid (powder or serum)
good: Holds water on the skin's surface for a plump, hydrated feel.
care: Needs water to dissolve, so a homemade serum also needs a preservative. Store-bought serums are usually the safer route.

name: Panthenol (vitamin B5)
good: Hydrates and soothes. Used at 1% to 5%.
care: Low risk. Water-soluble.

name: Sodium PCA
good: A humectant that's part of the skin's own moisture factor.
care: Low risk at 1% to 3%.

name: Vitamin C powder (ascorbic acid)
care: It breaks down within days once mixed with water, turning yellow or brown, and at effective strengths it stings. A well-made store serum is more reliable.

name: Coenzyme Q10
good: Antioxidant used in small amounts in creams.
care: Low risk. Turns products yellow.

name: Bakuchiol
good: A gentle plant alternative to retinol, with early evidence for fine lines at 0.5% to 1%.
care: Generally well tolerated. Expensive; buy from a cosmetic supplier.

name: Allantoin
good: Soothes and softens at 0.1% to 0.5%.
care: Low risk. Dissolves poorly; use warm water.

name: Rosemary extract (ROE)
good: Slows oils going rancid, like vitamin E.
care: An antioxidant, not a preservative. It doesn't stop mold.

name: Leucidal (radish root ferment)
flag: Leucidal alone is a weak preservative
care: It often fails lab preservative tests when used on its own. Pair it with another preservative or choose a proven broad-spectrum one.

name: Cetearyl alcohol
good: A fatty alcohol that thickens creams. Not drying, despite the name.
care: Low risk. Works with an emulsifier; it doesn't emulsify well alone.

name: Fruit enzyme powder (papain, bromelain)
good: Gentle exfoliation in rinse-off masks.
care: Strength varies by batch. Rinse within 10 minutes and stop if it stings.

name: Zinc oxide
flag: You can't make reliable sunscreen at home
care: Fine as a soothing powder in diaper creams and balms. But homemade sunscreens can't be tested for SPF and usually protect far less than you'd expect. Avoid inhaling the loose powder.

name: Coconut milk powder
good: Creamy, softening powder for masks and bath soaks.
care: Low risk. Mix fresh; once wet it spoils like milk.

name: Magnesium hydroxide
good: A gentle odor-neutralizer for deodorants, much less irritating than baking soda.
care: Low risk. Use cosmetic grade.

name: Zinc ricinoleate
good: Traps odor molecules in deodorants.
care: Low risk at 1% to 3%.

name: Polysorbate 20 (solubilizer)
good: Lets fragrance or essential oil disperse in water-based mists.
care: Low risk. Usually used at 1 to 3 parts per part of fragrance.

name: Alum (fitkari, potassium alum)
good: Traditional astringent, used as an aftershave block and crystal deodorant.
care: Stings cuts and freshly shaved skin. It isn't soap and doesn't cleanse.

name: Marine collagen powder
good: A supplement sold to drink.
care: On skin, collagen molecules are too large to soak in, so they can't build collagen. Made from fish; avoid with a fish allergy. Dissolved in water, it spoils.

name: Freeze-dried fruit powder
good: Color and scent in dry scrubs, without fresh fruit's water.
care: Keep dry. Can stain lightly.

name: Black seed (nigella) oil
good: Popular in hair and brow oils.
care: A known cause of allergic rashes. Patch test, and keep it out of the eyes.

name: Caffeine (oil-soluble or powder)
good: Can briefly reduce under-eye puffiness by narrowing surface blood vessels.
care: The effect is temporary and small. It doesn't remove dark circles from pigment or genetics.

name: Emulsifying wax (e.g. Polawax, Olivem)
good: Binds oil and water into a stable lotion. Beeswax can't do this on its own.
care: Creams with water still need a broad-spectrum preservative.

name: Pearl powder (cosmetic grade)
good: Gives creams a soft, luminous finish.
care: The glow is optical. Claims that it whitens skin aren't backed by good evidence.

name: Ceramide liposome or ceramide complex
good: Supports the skin barrier in well-made creams.
care: A lab ingredient, usually sold in a water base that needs a preservative. Follow the supplier's percentage.

name: Niacinamide powder (vitamin B3)
good: Well studied for oil control, redness, and pore appearance at 2% to 5%.
care: More isn't better: above 5% it often causes redness and flushing. Weigh it on a 0.01 g scale. Dissolved in water, it needs a preservative if stored.

name: Sugar (white or brown)
good: Classic body scrub base. Dissolves as you rinse.
care: Too sharp for the face. Body only, never on broken skin.

name: Salt (sea or table)
good: Body scrub base.
care: Stings cuts and freshly shaved skin. Body only.

name: Coffee grounds (used or fresh)
good: Invigorating body scrub.
care: Coarse, so body only. Wet grounds mold quickly; dry them before storing.

name: Cinnamon powder
care: A common cause of burning and allergic rashes. Keep it off the face and lips.

name: Activated charcoal
good: Popular in clay masks for oily skin.
care: Messy and stains grout and towels. Never use it in glue-based peel-off masks.

name: Dried hibiscus
good: Ground hibiscus adds color and a fine, gentle texture to scrubs and masks.
care: Can tint skin and towels pink for a while. Mold grows on it if it gets wet.

name: Dried jasmine flowers
good: Adds a light floral scent to scrubs and infused oils.
care: Jasmine is a known fragrance allergen for some people. Keep it dry.

name: Dried rose petals or buds
good: Gentle and pretty in scrubs, bath soaks, and infused oils.
care: Use only fully dried petals. Fresh petals carry water into oil, where mold grows. Strain them out of infused oils.

name: Curry leaves (fresh or dried)
care: Fresh leaves carry water into oil, where mold grows. Cook them until crisp before straining. There's no good evidence they prevent grey hair.

name: Blue lotus flowers
flag: Blue lotus is mostly sold for other uses
care: Much blue lotus is marketed as a smokable or drinkable relaxant, and its skincare evidence is minimal. Buy cosmetic-grade if you use it.

name: Calendula (marigold) petals
good: A classic gentle herb for salves and infused oils.
care: Can trigger reactions in people allergic to daisies or ragweed.

name: Black seed (nigella, kalonji)
good: Common in hair oils and Middle Eastern and South Asian remedies.
care: Black seed oil can cause allergic rashes in some people; patch test.

name: Dried nettle leaf
good: Used in hair rinses and oils.
care: Fresh nettle stings. Use it dried or cooked.

name: Star anise
good: Warm scent in infused hair oils.
care: Fine as a whole spice. Star anise essential oil is a strong allergen.

name: Dried thyme
good: Herbal scent in infused oils and rinses.
care: Fine dried. Thyme essential oil is very irritating on skin.

name: Butterfly pea flowers (aparajita)
good: Gives a vivid blue color to gels and hair rinses.
care: Can tint light hair and skin slightly blue. The hair growth and anti-greying claims are traditional, not proven.

name: Fresh herbs (rosemary, mint, basil)
flag: Dry or fry fresh herbs before infusing
care: Fresh leaves carry water into oil, where mould, bacteria and even botulism spores can grow; gentle heat (50 to 60°C) doesn't kill them. Use fully dried herbs for an oil you keep, or keep a fresh-herb oil in the fridge and use it within 2 to 4 days.

name: Bay leaves
good: Common in infused hair oils.
care: Low risk dried.

name: Cumin seeds
good: Warm scent in infused oils.
care: Low risk as a whole seed.

name: Cinnamon sticks (infused)
care: Cinnamon is a common cause of skin burning and allergy, and infusing pulls it into the oil. Keep it out of face products and patch test the scalp.

name: Saw palmetto
good: Popular in hair loss blends.
care: The hair studies used it taken by mouth, mostly in men. There's little evidence it works on the scalp.

name: Marshmallow root
good: Makes a slippery, detangling hair rinse.
care: Low risk. Water infusions spoil within a day or two.

name: Dried rosemary
good: The herb, not the essential oil. Common in infused hair oils.
care: Low risk dried.

name: Horsetail
good: Popular in hair rinses and teas.
care: The silica claims for hair aren't backed by good evidence. Don't drink it long-term; it can deplete vitamin B1.

name: Burdock root
good: Traditional in scalp oils and rinses.
care: Can cause reactions in people allergic to daisies or ragweed.

name: Flaxseed (whole, infused in oil)
good: Adds a little body to infused oils.
care: Low risk. Boil in water instead to make flaxseed gel.

name: Dried grated carrot
good: For making carrot-infused oil.
care: Dry it completely before adding oil. Any moisture left can grow mold.

name: Chebe powder
good: Chadian seed and spice blend used to coat hair lengths and reduce breakage.
care: Applied to hair, not the scalp. Blends vary; patch test the scalp if it gets there.

name: Dried sage
good: Herbal hair rinses and oils.
care: Low risk dried. Sage essential oil is a different, stronger product.

name: Yarrow
good: Traditional in scalp rinses.
care: Can trigger reactions in people allergic to daisies or ragweed.

name: Fennel seeds
good: Warm scent in infused oils.
care: Low risk as whole seed.

name: Coriander seeds
good: Spice used in infused hair oils.
care: Low risk.

name: Dried basil
good: Herbal scent in hair oils.
care: Low risk dried.

name: Dried mint powder
good: Fresh flavor in tooth powders and face packs.
care: Low risk.

name: Clove powder
care: Ground clove is strong. Traditional for gums in small amounts, but keep it off the face.

name: Dried oregano
good: Herb used in some infused hair oils.
care: Fine dried. Oregano essential oil is one of the most irritating oils on skin; never use it undiluted.

name: Dried onion flakes
care: Drying first is the right call, since fresh onion carries water into oil. It can still sting a scratched scalp; patch test.

name: Dried papaya seeds
good: Infused into oil for body and face blends.
care: Dry them completely before infusing. The dark-spot claims aren't backed by studies.

name: Dried lavender buds
good: Scent and color in bath soaks, teas, and infused oils.
care: Low risk. Loose buds clog drains; bag them.

name: Dried chamomile flowers
good: Gentle, soothing flower for bath teas and infused oils.
care: Can trigger reactions in people allergic to ragweed or daisies.

name: Lemon balm leaves
good: Light lemony scent in bath teas.
care: Low risk.

name: Dried spearmint or peppermint leaves
good: Fresh scent in bath teas and foot soaks.
care: Much gentler than mint essential oil.

name: Lemon verbena leaves
good: Bright lemon scent.
care: Low risk dried. Lemon verbena essential oil is a strong allergen.

name: Oatstraw
good: Gentle, softening herb for bath teas.
care: Low risk.

name: Dried eucalyptus leaves
good: Fresh scent in bath teas and shower bundles.
care: Milder than the essential oil. Keep away from young children's faces.

name: Dried lemongrass
good: Citrusy scent in bath teas.
care: Low risk dried.

name: Patchouli leaves
good: Earthy scent for bath blends.
care: Low risk.

name: Vetiver (khus) root
good: Earthy-scented root used in traditional bath powders and hair oils.
care: Low risk dried.

name: Avarampoo (tanner's cassia flower)
good: Traditional South Indian flower for bath powders.
care: Low risk dried. Patch test, as with any plant.

name: Whole cloves (infused in oil)
care: Steeping cloves in oil or water pulls out eugenol, the same irritant that makes clove essential oil one of the harshest on skin. A home infusion's strength can't be measured, so keep it off the face and lips.

name: Lavender essential oil
good: Pleasant and widely tolerated.
care: Becomes more irritating as it ages. Keep capped and cool, and replace after 1 to 2 years.

name: Tea tree essential oil
good: Studied for acne in diluted gels.
care: Old, oxidized tea tree oil is a known cause of skin allergy. Store cool and dark.

name: Frankincense (boswellia) essential oil
good: Warm, resinous scent. Generally well tolerated; a classic in face oils and body oils at 1% or less.
care: Oxidizes with age and air, and old oil is more likely to irritate. Buy small, keep it capped, dark and cool, and use within about a year of opening. Scent, not a skin toner.

name: German chamomile essential oil
good: Among the gentlest essential oils.
care: Can trigger reactions in people allergic to ragweed or daisies.

name: Geranium essential oil
good: Floral scent, common in face blends.
care: Can irritate at higher amounts.

name: Sweet orange essential oil
good: Bright scent and not sun-sensitizing.
care: Oxidizes fast once opened. Use within a year.

name: Rose essential oil (otto or absolute)
good: Classic floral scent, used in tiny amounts.
care: Very expensive, so it's often diluted or faked. Contains natural allergens; keep it low.

name: Sandalwood essential oil
good: Warm, woody scent that's generally well tolerated.
care: Indian sandalwood is overharvested and often adulterated; Australian sandalwood is a more sustainable choice.

name: Carrot seed essential oil
good: Earthy oil common in face and body blends.
care: This is an essential oil, not the same as infused carrot oil, so it counts toward essential oil limits.

name: Baking extract (vanilla, peppermint)
flag: Baking extracts don't mix with oil
care: Kitchen extracts are mostly alcohol and water. In an oil scrub they separate, add water to the jar, and can sting. Use a skin-safe fragrance or flavor oil instead.

name: Attar (traditional perfume oil)
good: Concentrated floral perfume, often jasmine or rose in sandalwood oil.
care: Strength and contents vary a lot. Use a small amount and patch test.

name: Lip-safe flavor oil
good: Adds taste and scent to lip products.
care: Use flavor made for lip products, not baking extracts (they contain alcohol and water) or candle fragrance. About 1% is plenty.

name: Fragrance oil (cosmetic grade)
good: Adds scent at low cost.
care: Use only cosmetic-grade fragrance with a stated skin-safe rate, never candle fragrance. A common cause of skin allergy.

name: Cosmetic mica powder
good: Adds shimmer and color.
care: Use cosmetic-grade mica only. Craft glitter and non-cosmetic pigments aren't skin-safe. Keep loose powder out of the eyes.

name: Turmeric essential oil
good: Warm, spicy scent. Stains far less than turmeric powder.
care: Can irritate at higher amounts. Keep it low in face products.

name: Blue tansy essential oil
good: Deep blue oil popular in calming face blends.
care: Stains skin, towels, and pillowcases blue. Related to ragweed, so it can trigger reactions in people with that allergy. Very expensive and often adulterated.

name: Lemongrass essential oil
good: Fresh, lemony scent popular in soaps.
care: Rich in citral, a common skin allergen. Keep it at or below 0.7% in leave-on products.

name: Cedarwood essential oil
good: Warm, woody base note for perfumes and beard oils.
care: Generally well tolerated.

name: Ylang ylang essential oil
good: Rich floral scent.
care: A known skin sensitizer. Keep it at or below 0.8%.

name: Jasmine absolute
good: Intense floral scent, used in tiny amounts.
care: A known skin allergen. Keep it at or below 0.7%. Very expensive and often faked.

name: Clary sage essential oil
good: Herbal, musky scent.
care: Many references advise avoiding it during pregnancy.

name: Patchouli essential oil
good: Earthy base note that makes blends last longer.
care: Generally well tolerated. Strong; a little goes a long way.

name: Hyssop essential oil
good: Herbal scent.
care: Contains pinocamphone, which can trigger seizures at high doses. Avoid during pregnancy, with epilepsy, and in children's products.

name: Citronella essential oil
good: Lemony scent, best known as an insect repellent.
care: Can irritate and sensitize skin. Keep it low.

name: Vanilla absolute or CO2 extract
good: Warm, sweet scent.
care: There's no true vanilla essential oil. Products sold under that name are an absolute, a CO2 extract, an oleoresin, or a fragrance oil. Check which you have.

name: Lemon or grapefruit oil (steam-distilled or FCF)
good: Citrus scent without the sun-sensitizing compounds.
care: Check the label says steam-distilled or FCF. Oxidizes quickly once opened.

name: Cocoa absolute
good: Rich chocolate scent.
care: Very concentrated. Use only a drop or two.

name: Helichrysum essential oil
good: Popular in face blends for scars and fine lines.
care: Generally gentle. Very expensive and often adulterated; the scar claims are mostly traditional.

name: Neroli essential oil
good: Soft floral scent from orange blossom; not sun-sensitizing.
care: Expensive and often diluted or faked. Patch test.

name: Vetiver essential oil
good: Deep, earthy base note.
care: Low risk at normal amounts.

name: Hinoki (Japanese cypress) essential oil
good: Woody, fresh scent used in Japanese bath products.
care: Oxidizes over time; use within a year.

name: Black pepper essential oil
good: Warming scent used in muscle rubs.
care: Can irritate when it's old and oxidized. Keep it under 1% and off the face.

name: Sweet marjoram essential oil
good: Warm, herbal scent popular in muscle and sleep blends.
care: Low risk at normal amounts.

name: Elemi essential oil
good: Fresh, lemony-resin scent used in skin and scar blends.
care: Low risk at normal amounts. Oxidizes with age.

name: Palmarosa essential oil
good: Rosy, grassy scent popular in dry-skin blends.
care: Low risk at normal amounts.

name: Litsea (may chang) essential oil
good: Bright lemony scent that isn't sun-sensitizing.
care: High in citral, a common skin sensitizer. Keep it under 0.8% in leave-on products.

name: Cassia essential oil
care: Like cinnamon bark, one of the most irritating oils. Max 0.05% on the body, never on lips or face.

name: Ginger essential oil
good: Warming scent for muscle rubs.
care: Low risk at normal amounts; keep off the face.

name: Cardamom essential oil
good: Sweet, spicy scent.
care: Low risk at normal amounts. Not for the face of young children.

name: Nutmeg essential oil
care: Contains myristicin. Keep it under 0.8% and avoid it in pregnancy.

name: Vanilla absolute
good: Warm, true vanilla scent that blends into oils.
care: Can sensitize some people. Keep it around 1% or less.

name: Juniper berry essential oil
good: Fresh, woody scent for body scrubs and soaks.
care: Can irritate when oxidized. Use fresh oil.

name: Cypress essential oil
good: Green, woody scent.
care: Low risk at normal amounts; can irritate when oxidized.

name: Myrrh essential oil
good: Warm, resinous scent used in face blends.
care: Many aromatherapy references advise avoiding it during pregnancy.

name: Rosemary essential oil
good: Herbal scent, popular in hair and body products.
care: Not for use near the face of children under 6.

name: Peppermint essential oil
good: Cooling in body and foot products.
care: Keep away from eyes. Not for children under 6 near the face, where it can affect breathing.

name: Eucalyptus essential oil
good: Fresh scent for body products.
care: Not for children under 6 near the face, where it can affect breathing.

name: Bergamot essential oil (not FCF)
good: Popular citrus-floral scent.
care: Causes burns and dark patches in sunlight. Max 0.4% in leave-on products, or buy the FCF version.

name: Lemon essential oil (cold-pressed)
good: Fresh citrus scent.
care: Sun-sensitizing. Max 2% in leave-on products; steam-distilled lemon oil doesn't have this problem.

name: Lime essential oil (cold-pressed)
good: Sharp citrus scent.
care: Sun-sensitizing. Max 0.7% in leave-on products.

name: Grapefruit essential oil
good: Light citrus scent.
care: Mildly sun-sensitizing. Max 4% in leave-on products.

name: Cinnamon bark essential oil
care: One of the most irritating essential oils. Max 0.07% on the body and never on face or lips.

name: Clove bud essential oil
care: Strongly irritating. Max 0.5% on the body and never on face or lips.

name: Geogard ECT (broad-spectrum preservative)
good: A preservative accepted in natural and organic certifications. Needed in anything with water that you store.
care: Use 0.4% to 1% of the total weight, measured on a scale that reads 0.01 g.

name: Vitamin E (tocopherol)
good: Slows oils from going rancid at 0.2% to 1%.
care: An antioxidant, not a preservative. It does nothing against mold or bacteria.

name: Grapefruit seed extract
flag: Grapefruit seed extract isn't a preservative
care: It isn't a reliable preservative. Lab tests traced its effect to synthetic preservatives added during manufacturing.

name: Olivem 1000 (plant emulsifier)
good: Binds oil and water into a stable lotion or cream.
care: Lotion making needs heat, a scale, and a preservative.

name: Shower gel, liquid soap, or castile soap
good: Turns an oil scrub into a foaming scrub that rinses clean.
care: It's mostly water. Mixed into a jar of scrub, its preservative gets diluted and the jar can grow mold in a wet shower. Add a squirt to each scoop as you use it instead.

name: Moroccan black soap (savon beldi)
good: Soft olive-oil soap used in hammam routines before a kessa glove scrub.
care: Alkaline, so keep it out of eyes and rinse well. Can dry the face; 1 to 2 minutes is enough there.

name: African black soap (alata samina)
good: Ghanaian soap made from plant ash and shea butter.
care: Strongly alkaline and can be drying. Lather it in your hands rather than rubbing the bar on skin, since bits of ash can scratch.

name: Melt-and-pour soap base
good: Ready-made soap you melt, scent, and pour. The safe way to make bars without handling lye.
care: Keep essential oils within the supplier's rate, usually 1% to 3%.

name: Hair bleaching powder (persulfate)
good: Lightens body hair as part of a banho de lua.
care: Persulfates can cause allergic reactions that appear hours later, and breathing in the powder irritates the lungs. Use a cream bleach kit made for body hair and follow its instructions.

name: Peroxide cream developer (água oxigenada)
good: Activates bleaching powder.
care: 20 volume (6%) is the usual strength for body hair; 30 volume is strong for skin. Never on broken, sunburned, or freshly shaved skin.

name: Melt-and-pour shampoo bar base
good: Ready-made base for solid shampoo bars, without handling lye.
care: Keep essential oils within the supplier's rate, usually up to 2% for hair.

name: Sodium lactate
good: Makes cold process soap bars harder and easier to unmold, at about 1% of oils.
care: Low risk. Add it to the cooled lye water.

name: Carbomer (gel thickener)
good: Turns water and aloe into a clear gel at about 0.5%.
care: It only thickens after it's neutralized. Use a ready-made neutralizer such as triethanolamine or aminomethyl propanol, never lye you've mixed yourself.

name: Kojic acid
good: A tested dark-spot ingredient in leave-on products at about 1%.
care: Can irritate and cause allergies. It breaks down and turns brown in soap and in heat, so in a rinse-off bar it does very little.

name: Slippery elm bark powder
good: Turns slippery when wet, so hair masks spread and detangle more easily.
care: Low risk on skin and hair. Spoils like any wet herb mask once mixed.

name: Calcium carbonate (chalk powder)
good: The gentle polishing powder used in many store toothpastes.
care: Mildly abrasive; brush gently. Buy food or cosmetic grade.

name: Babassu oil
good: Light Brazilian oil that behaves like coconut oil, with a less greasy feel.
care: Can clog pores on the face for some people, like coconut oil.

name: Borneol (bing pian)
care: A camphor relative used in Chinese balms. It's toxic if swallowed and can affect breathing in young children. Keep it under 1%, off the face, and away from children under 6 and during pregnancy.

name: Sodium cocoyl isethionate (SCI)
good: A mild, coconut-derived cleanser that makes solid shampoo bars lather.
care: Wear a mask when handling the fine powder; it irritates the nose and lungs.

name: BTMS (behentrimonium methosulfate)
good: The conditioning emulsifier behind most conditioner bars. Detangles and smooths.
care: Low risk in rinse-off products. Keep it out of eyes.

name: Alpha arbutin
good: A gentle brightening active, used at about 1 to 2% in leave-on serums.
care: Works in leave-on products; in a scrub it rinses off before it can do much.

name: Chebe-infused oil
good: Oil infused with Chadian chebe powder, used to coat and protect hair lengths.
care: Helps hold length by reducing breakage; it doesn't make hair grow faster.

name: Lightening milk or lotion (unlabelled)
flag: Check what's in the lightening milk
care: Unlabelled lightening lotions sold in some markets have been found to contain hydroquinone, mercury, or steroid creams, which can cause lasting damage. Use only a product that lists every ingredient, and avoid those three.

name: Dried mugwort (ssuk, ai ye)
flag: Mugwort: skip in pregnancy and with ragweed allergy
good: Traditional Korean and Chinese bath and steam herb with a warm, earthy scent.
care: Mugwort is traditionally used to bring on periods, so avoid it in pregnancy. It's in the daisy family and a common pollen allergen; skip it if ragweed or chamomile bothers you.

name: Frankincense resin (refined or tears)
good: Resin that partly dissolves into warm oil, adding a soft, woody note.
care: Boswellic acid is studied as a supplement for joints; there's little evidence it does anything on skin. Strain out undissolved bits.

name: Dead Sea salt
good: Magnesium-rich salt. In a small study, a 15-minute soak in a 5% solution improved hydration and roughness in dry, eczema-prone skin.
care: Stings cracked, weeping or freshly scratched skin. A handful in a full tub is far weaker than the 5% studied.

name: Plantain leaf (Plantago)
good: Its slippery mucilage coats raw, scratched skin. Germany's Commission E approved ribwort plantain for mild skin inflammation.
care: Low risk. This is the garden weed, not the banana-like plantain fruit.

name: Tamarind pulp
good: Contains tartaric acid, a mild AHA, so it adds a gentle exfoliating effect to body scrubs and masks.
care: Food: use right away. Can sting freshly shaved skin. Rinse within 10 minutes.

name: Alginate modeling (rubber) mask powder
good: Seaweed-based powder that sets into a cool, rubbery peel-off mask and holds moisture against the skin.
care: The de-puffing is short-lived cooling. Keep it out of eyebrows and hairline, and leave the nostrils and mouth clear.

name: Bamboo salt (jukyeom)
good: Korean sea salt roasted inside bamboo. Works like any salt in a gargle or rinse.
care: Claims that it detoxes or treats illness aren't backed by research. Gargle and spit; swallowing adds salt, which matters with high blood pressure.

name: Plain kefir
good: Fermented milk with gentle lactic acid, like a thinner yogurt. A soft, mildly exfoliating mask for face or hair.
care: Use plain, unsweetened kefir; flavored ones add sugar and fruit flavorings. Food: use right away and rinse within 15 minutes. Skip with a dairy allergy.

name: Brewed chamomile tea, cooled
good: A cooled tea compress soothes and calms warm, irritated skin.
care: Spoils like any drink, so make it fresh. Not sterile, so clean cuts with clean water instead. Ragweed or daisy allergy risk.

name: Reishi or tremella mushroom (dried)
good: Tremella holds water like hyaluronic acid in lab tests; reishi is a traditional calming tonic. Pleasant in bath teas.
care: Bath water this dilute does very little beyond the warm soak. Mushroom allergy is rare but possible.

name: Dried osmanthus or honeysuckle flowers
good: Sweet, apricot-like scent; classic in Chinese teas and bath blends.
care: Low risk. Mostly there for fragrance.

name: Bergamot essential oil, FCF (bergapten-free)
good: Bright citrus-floral scent without the sun-burn risk of regular bergamot.
care: Check the label says FCF or bergapten-free. Oxidizes over time, so keep it capped and cool.

name: Beetroot powder
good: Dried beet gives a soft pink tint to balms and blushes.
care: It doesn't dissolve in oil, so sift it very fine or it feels gritty. The tint is sheer and can fade or turn brownish over weeks.

name: Guava leaves (fresh or dried)
good: Traditional across the Caribbean, Latin America and Southeast Asia as a hair rinse and tea. Rich in tannins and antioxidants, which give a slightly tightening, clean feel.
care: Hair-growth claims come from personal stories and lab tests, not trials. Use the leaves only: guava bark is traditionally warned against in pregnancy. Water infusions spoil within a day or two.

name: Unscented body wash base
good: Ready-made, preserved soap base you can scent at home.
care: Add fragrance at 0.5 to 1% at most, and don't add water, milk or fresh ingredients, which dilute the preservative.

name: Mango leaves (fresh or dried)
good: Young mango leaves contain mangiferin, an antioxidant. Used in Caribbean, South Asian and Pacific traditions as a rinse and tea.
care: The hair-growth studies on mangiferin are lab and animal work, not human trials. Mango is related to poison ivy, so people allergic to mango skin or sap should patch test.

name: Vanilla bean (whole or split)
good: Infused into butters and oils for a warm, sweet scent. Origins smell different: Madagascar (Bourbon) is creamy and classic, Tahitian is floral and cherry-like (a different species), Mexican is spicy and woody, Ugandan is rich and chocolatey with high vanillin.
care: Buy from reputable sellers; cheap "Mexican vanilla" extracts have been found cut with coumarin (tonka). Strain the bean out for anything kept long; infused oils hold scent but not much else.

name: Camwood powder (uhie, osun, Baphia nitida)
good: West African red-orange wood powder used for a warm glow on skin and a blush on lips, and in ceremonies. Lab studies show antioxidant and antimicrobial compounds.
care: Tints skin, nails and fabric orange for a day or two. Patch test; buy it from sellers who don't mix in dyes.

name: Nzu, efun or orhue (white clay)
good: Nigerian white clay used as a cooling, matte paste on skin and in ceremonies, much like kaolin.
care: For skin only. Eating nzu, which some people do in pregnancy, is unsafe: samples have contained lead and arsenic, and it can block iron absorption.

name: Indigo powder (Indigofera)
good: Natural blue dye used for body patterns and, after henna, to darken hair. Indigo naturalis ointment has been studied for psoriasis.
care: Stains skin and nails blue for days. Real indigo is never "black henna"; avoid anything that turns black within an hour, which may contain PPD.

name: Uli dye (Igbo body art)
good: Plant dye painted in fine patterns on skin by Igbo women; it darkens over a day and fades in about a week.
care: Little is known about its safety on skin, and blends vary. Patch test and keep it off the lips, eyes and broken skin.

name: White Flower oil (embrocation)
good: A strong menthol, camphor, eucalyptus and wintergreen rub for sore muscles and headaches.
care: Wintergreen is methyl salicylate, related to aspirin; a small amount swallowed is dangerous for children. Not for under-6s, not near eyes or on broken skin, and check with a doctor if you take blood thinners.

name: Ximenia (sour plum) oil
good: A rich kernel oil from the Sahel and southern Africa, traditionally used to condition hair and protect skin from dry wind. Contains ximenynic acid, an unusual fatty acid.
care: Claims that it boosts blood flow or regulates oil come from small, mostly brand-funded studies. Treat it as a good, stable emollient.

name: Safou (African pear, ube) pulp oil
good: Oil from the buttery pulp of Dacryodes edulis, eaten across West and Central Africa. Rich in oleic and palmitic acids, so it softens skin and adds gloss to hair.
care: Little cosmetic research yet and hard to buy refined. Patch test, and treat it like olive oil on acne-prone faces.

name: Kpangnan butter (Pentadesma)
good: A golden West African butter, softer than shea, that melts quickly on contact. Good for balms and whipped butters.
care: Very rich; can clog pores on the face. Store cool.

name: Kigelia (sausage tree) fruit extract
good: Used in traditional African poultices for skin conditions; extracts show antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects in lab studies.
care: Firming and anti-aging claims rest on lab work. Some extracts show hormone-like activity, which is a reason for caution, not a selling point; skip it in pregnancy. Don't use raw unripe fruit, which is irritating.

name: Resurrection plant (Myrothamnus) extract
good: A southern African plant that revives after drought; its extract contains trehalose, a sugar that helps hold water, plus antioxidants.
care: The cell-protection studies were done in lab dishes. In a toner it works as a humectant; it contains some arbutin, so patch test.

name: Atile resin (African elemi, Canarium)
good: Fragrant resin from the atile tree (ube mgba), used in West African balms and as a perfume fixative.
care: Resins and elemi can cause skin allergies, especially as they age. Use a small amount in balms, patch test, and keep it off the face.

name: Prekese (aidan) pods
good: Aromatic West African pods used in soups, baths and traditional washes; contain saponins and fragrant oils.
care: Strong and can irritate; little is known about it on skin. Use as a diluted bath or rinse, not a leave-on, and patch test.

name: Ambunu leaves or powder
good: Chadian herb (Ceratotheca sesamoides). Steeped in warm water it turns slippery, which helps detangle and gently cleanse curly hair.
care: Low risk. Strain well so leaf bits don't tangle in hair, and use a fresh batch each time.

name: Perfumer's alcohol (ethanol 95%)
good: The base for spray perfumes and tinctures. It dissolves scent materials and evaporates cleanly.
care: For perfumes and tinctures only, not leave-on skincare; it dries skin. Very flammable: keep it capped and away from flames. Rubbing alcohol is not a substitute.

name: Xylitol powder
good: A sugar alcohol that cavity bacteria can't feed on; sweetens tooth powders and pastes.
care: Safe for people, but very toxic to dogs even in small amounts. Store it where pets can't reach.

name: Breast milk
flag: Breast milk spoils like any milk
care: Lovely in a fresh bath or a soap where it's a small part of the bar. In a lotion or cream without a tested preservative it grows bacteria within days, which is a real risk on a baby's skin.

name: Cosmetic gold powder or flakes
good: Adds sparkle and a luxury feel.
care: Purely decorative: gold doesn't brighten, firm or fade spots. Use only cosmetic grade; craft glitter isn't skin-safe. Keep away from eyes.

name: Store-bought moisturizing cream (e.g. Nivea Creme)
good: Already preserved and tested; a reliable base for small add-ins.
care: Stir add-ins into a scoop in a clean jar, not the whole tub, so you don't dilute its preservative.

name: Lanolin (anhydrous)
good: Wool wax that seals and softens very dry lips, nipples and heels; it holds water like few other ingredients.
care: A known allergen for a small number of people, especially those with eczema. Patch test. Not vegan.

name: Dandelion (leaf, root or flower)
good: Traditional in herbal vinegars and teas.
care: Daisy family: skip with ragweed allergy. Pick only from unsprayed ground.

name: Mahlab (cherry kernel) powder
good: Ground kernels of the St Lucie cherry; sweet almond-cherry scent. A key note in Sudanese khumra and dilka.
care: Infuse in oil and strain, or use in rinse-off scrubs. Skip with a stone-fruit or almond allergy.

name: Myrrh resin (tears or powder)
good: Warm, bitter-sweet resin traditionally burned as incense and infused into oils and balms.
care: Only partly dissolves in warm oil; strain well. Can irritate sensitive skin, and many references advise avoiding myrrh in pregnancy. Burn as incense only in a ventilated room.

name: Musk perfume oil (white musk, synthetic)
good: Soft, clean, long-lasting base note; the backbone of khumra, attars and oil perfumes.
care: Modern musk is synthetic (real deer musk is banned in most places). Polycyclic musks like galaxolide build up in the environment, and some older nitro musks are restricted. Strength varies a lot, so treat it like a fragrance oil: 1% or less on skin, patch test, and keep it off the face and broken skin.

name: Ground apricot seed (shell) powder
flag: Apricot shell is a sharp exfoliant
good: Gritty, long-lasting scrub particles for rough feet, elbows and knees.
care: Crushed shell has jagged edges that can cause micro-tears; keep it off the face and use light pressure. Finer sugar or jojoba beads are gentler.

name: Glycolic acid (AHA)
good: Proven exfoliating acid; in leave-on lotions at 5 to 10% it smooths rough skin and bumps.
care: Don't combine with a physical scrub, use on shaved skin, or skip sunscreen after. Strength and pH matter, so buy it ready-made rather than adding powder at home.

name: Jute leaf (ewedu, mrenda, molokhia)
good: Corchorus leaves turn slippery when soaked or blended, which helps detangle and gently cleanse hair, like ambunu.
care: Not the same plant as Sida acuta, which looks similar; buy from someone who can name it. Use fresh, same day, and strain well.

name: Sandalwood chips or powder
good: Raw wood for tinctures, dilka and incense. Soaking crushed chips in perfumer's alcohol pulls out the warm, creamy scent slowly.
care: Much "sandalwood" sold cheaply is other wood with added fragrance. Buy from a seller who names the species (Santalum album or Santalum spicatum).

name: Black sesame seeds
flag: Sesame is a common food allergen
good: Used in East Asian and Ayurvedic hair oils. Infused in oil they add a nutty smell.
care: Sesame allergy can be serious, so skip if you react to sesame. There's no good evidence that eating or applying it darkens or regrows hair.

name: Black peppercorns (whole)
flag: Pepper can sting and redden the scalp
good: Added to some "growth" hair oils for a warming tingle.
care: Piperine irritates skin. The tingle is irritation, not proof it works. Keep it out of eyes and off broken or sensitive scalps.

name: Beef bone marrow fat (rendered, tutano)
good: Soft animal fat used in Brazilian tutano hair masks. Like tallow, it coats strands and slows moisture loss.
care: Raw marrow carries bacteria and goes rancid fast. Render it gently, strain out every bit of tissue, and keep it in the fridge. Strong smell; keep it off the face.

name: Pine bark (dried)
good: Rich in tannins and antioxidant polyphenols (the source of Pycnogenol). Used in some herbal mouth rinses.
care: Low risk as a tea. Buy food-grade bark, not garden mulch.

name: Hydroxyapatite (nano or micro)
good: The mineral teeth are made of. In toothpaste it helps remineralize early enamel weak spots; studies find it comparable to fluoride for that.
care: It doesn't dissolve, so shake rinses before use. Buy cosmetic or dental grade.

name: Borage seed oil
good: The richest plant source of GLA, a fatty acid that helps dry, rough skin hold moisture.
care: Goes rancid quickly. Buy small bottles, keep in the fridge, and add vitamin E.

name: Magnesium or zinc stearate
good: A silky powder that helps loose and pressed powders cling to skin and stop looking chalky. Zinc myristate in Suppin powder does the same job.
care: Use 3 to 5% of a powder. Very light and dusty, so don't breathe it in while mixing.

name: Silk or sericite powder
good: Gives powders a soft, blurring slip and a natural sheen instead of a flat, chalky finish.
care: Low risk. Silk is an animal product; sericite (a fine mica) is the vegan option.

name: Polysorbate 80
good: A stronger solubilizer than polysorbate 20. It lets oil turn milky and rinse away with water, which is how shower oils work.
care: Low risk at 10 to 20% of a shower oil. Sticky on its own; don't use it in leave-on oils.

name: Tapioca starch
good: A light, silky starch that absorbs sweat and stops chafing. Feels smoother than cornstarch and is used in talc-free body powders.
care: Low risk. Keep it dry; damp starch in skin folds can feed yeast, so apply only to fully dry skin.

name: Hydrolyzed rice protein
good: Small protein pieces that cling to damaged hair, filling gaps so strands feel thicker and break less. Works in shampoo and conditioner at 0.5 to 2%.
care: Too much protein can make fine or low-porosity hair stiff and straw-like; balance with moisture.

name: Biotin (vitamin B7) powder
good: Popular in "growth" hair products.
care: Low risk, but on hair or scalp it does nothing measurable. Biotin only helps hair if you're truly deficient, which is rare, and then by mouth. High-dose biotin supplements can throw off blood tests, including heart and thyroid tests.

name: Cooked sweet potato (mashed)
good: Thick, starchy base that helps a hair mask cling.
care: Food: use right away, never store. Mash and strain very smoothly or bits stick in hair.

name: Sulfur powder (precipitated)
flag: Sulfur can dry skin and smells strong
good: A real acne and fungal-acne active in leave-on products and masks (3 to 10%). It dries oily spots and calms dandruff and pityriasis versicolor.
care: In a rinse-off soap it has little time to work. Can dry and peel; avoid with a sulfa allergy and keep out of eyes. Buy cosmetic grade, never garden sulfur.

name: Food coloring (liquid or gel)
good: Easy color for melt-and-pour soap.
care: Food dyes aren't made for soap: they bleed, fade, can tint skin and towels, and some colors aren't approved for skin. Use soap-safe micas, oxides or natural powders (spirulina, beetroot, turmeric) instead.

name: Babchi (bakuchi seed) oil or powder
care: The whole seed contains psoralen, which makes skin burn, blister and darken in sunlight. Doctors use it only under supervision with controlled UV for vitiligo. Psoralens are banned in EU cosmetics. Bakuchiol is the purified, psoralen-free part; use that instead.

name: Soapnuts (reetha) shells
good: Boiled in water, the shells release saponins: a mild, low-lather natural cleanser used in Indian hair washes.
care: Stings badly in the eyes. The tea spoils within a day or two unless it's preserved.

name: Liquid shampoo base (unscented)
good: A ready-made, preserved shampoo you can scent or enrich.
care: Its preservative is balanced for the base alone. Adding herbal tea or water dilutes it, so add your own preservative as well.

name: Cosgard / Geogard 221 (benzyl alcohol, dehydroacetic acid)
good: Broad-spectrum preservative accepted in natural certifications. Works in shampoos, lotions and toners.
care: Use 0.6% to 1% of the total weight. Works best below pH 6. Benzyl alcohol is a listed fragrance allergen for a few people.

name: Amla hair oil (amla infused in sesame or coconut oil)
good: Traditional Indian hair oil for scalp massage and pre-wash treatments.
care: Many store versions add mineral oil or fragrance; check the label. The base is often coconut or sesame, so mind those allergies.

name: Hazelnut oil
good: One of the lightest, fastest-absorbing plant oils; a classic in dry oils and oily-skin blends.
care: Tree nut. Skip with a nut allergy. Goes rancid in about a year; add vitamin E.

name: Unflavoured gelatin
good: Sets liquid soap or body wash into a wobbly jelly soap.
care: Animal-derived, so not vegan; agar sets firmer and is the vegan swap. Protein plus water spoils, so anything made with gelatin and water belongs in the fridge.

name: Agarwood (oud) chips
good: Resin-soaked wood that gives oud its deep, smoky, leathery scent. Soak ground chips in perfumer's alcohol for a home oud tincture.
care: Wild agarwood trees (Aquilaria) are endangered and trade is restricted, so buy cultivated, plantation-grown chips from a seller who says so. Cheap 'oud' chips are often dyed or oil-soaked fakes.

name: High-proof spirit (rice spirit or vodka, 40 to 65%)
good: Pulls scent and plant compounds out of dried herbs for tinctures and hair tonics.
care: Strong alcohol dries and stings the scalp. Dilute a tincture with water or hydrosol before use, and keep it at least 20% alcohol so it doesn't spoil. Flammable.

name: Ginseng root (nhân sâm), dried
good: Traditional tonic root in East Asian hair tonics. Small studies suggest red ginseng may help alongside standard hair-loss treatment.
care: Low risk on the scalp. The evidence is limited, and mostly for ginseng taken by mouth.

name: Arborvitae leaf (trắc bách diệp, Platycladus), dried
good: A classic in Chinese and Vietnamese hair-loss tonics. Mouse studies show it can push hair into its growth phase.
care: No human trials yet. Its aromatic oils can irritate sensitive scalps; patch test, and keep it out of the eyes.

name: Fo-ti root (hà thủ ô), processed
good: The best-known Eastern herb for greying and thinning hair, used in tonics and dyes.
care: Taken by mouth, fo-ti has caused liver injury, so never drink it. On the scalp it's lower risk, but allergic rashes are reported. The anti-grey and growth claims are traditional, not proven. Patch test.

name: Dong quai root (đương quy, Angelica sinensis)
flag: Dong quai can make skin sun-sensitive
good: A warming 'blood-moving' root in Chinese hair and skin tonics.
care: Contains furocoumarins, which can make skin burn or darken in the sun. Use it in rinse-off products or on the scalp only, not the face.

name: Szechuan lovage root (xuyên khung, chuanxiong)
good: Usually paired with dong quai in Chinese tonics; aromatic and warming.
care: Low risk in a diluted tonic. No hair-growth trials.

name: Ku shen root (khổ sâm, Sophora flavescens)
good: A bitter root used for itchy, flaky scalps. Lab tests show antifungal activity.
care: Strong and can irritate. Use only a small amount in a diluted tonic or rinse, and never drink it.

name: Glossy privet fruit (nữ trinh tử, Ligustrum lucidum)
good: Small dark berries used in Chinese tonics for greying hair.
care: Low risk on the scalp. Hair claims are traditional only. The berries are poisonous to eat raw.

name: Red sage root (đan sâm, Salvia miltiorrhiza)
good: A circulation herb in Chinese medicine. Its tanshinones are studied for acne and inflammation in the lab.
care: Low risk in a diluted tonic. It can stain light hair and fabric red-brown.

name: Drynaria rhizome (cốt toái bổ, gu sui bu)
good: Traditionally used for bones; Chinese folk medicine also uses it in tonics for patchy hair loss.
care: Low risk on the scalp. No good human evidence for hair.

name: Safflower petals (hồng hoa)
good: Bright red-orange petals that colour tonics and oils; a 'blood-moving' herb in Chinese medicine.
care: Stains. Avoid in pregnancy (traditionally said to stimulate the uterus). Not the same as safflower cooking oil.

name: Red raspberry seed oil
good: Light, silky face oil rich in linoleic acid and vitamin E.
care: Its famous 'natural SPF 28 to 50' claim comes from a misread lab test; it is not a sunscreen. Goes rancid fairly quickly, so keep it cool and dark.

name: Neem leaves, dried (lá sầu đâu)
good: Infused into hair oils and rinses for itchy, flaky scalps; neem has antifungal activity in lab tests.
care: Smells strong and bitter. Lower risk than neem oil, but still patch test.

name: Comfrey leaf, dried
good: A traditional salve herb with some evidence for bruises, sprains and sore muscles on unbroken skin.
care: Contains pyrrolizidine alkaloids, which can harm the liver if absorbed. Use only on intact skin, for short periods (up to about 10 days), never on cuts, scrapes or broken skin, never inside the nose or mouth, and not in pregnancy, breastfeeding or on young children.

name: Sangre de drago (dragon's blood, Croton lechleri resin)
flag: Dragon's blood is for small, clean scrapes only
good: A red Amazonian tree sap that dries into a film over small scrapes and bites. Its compound taspine helped wound closure in lab and animal studies, and a drug made from it (crofelemer) is approved, though for diarrhoea, taken by mouth.
care: Small, cleaned scrapes and bites only; never deep, dirty or infected wounds. Stains skin and fabric dark red. Patch test; stop if redness spreads.

name: Black iron oxide (CI 77499)
good: The standard black pigment in store mascara and eyeliner, approved for the eye area in the US and EU.
care: Buy cosmetic grade. Wear a mask while measuring loose powder.

name: Cocamidopropyl betaine (CAPB)
good: Mild coconut-derived cleanser that softens harsher soaps and adds creamy foam.
care: It's sold as a water-based liquid, so anything it goes into needs a preservative. A few people react to it.

name: Kojic dipalmitate
good: Oil-soluble, more stable form of kojic acid for leave-on creams and oils.
care: Evidence for dark spots is weaker than for kojic acid. In a body wash it rinses straight off, so it's wasted there.

name: Chamomile-infused oil
good: Carrier oil (almond or jojoba) soaked with dried chamomile flowers. Gentle and soothing.
care: Use fully dried flowers so no water gets in. Skip if you're allergic to ragweed or daisies.

name: Coconut water (fresh)
good: Light, refreshing hair or skin rinse.
care: Food: it's mostly water and sugar, spoils within a day and can leave hair sticky. Use right away, never store.

name: Heavy whipping cream (dairy)
good: Blended long enough, it turns into plain dairy butter, a rich fat for a pre-wash hair mask.
care: Food: it goes rancid and sour-smelling, and leftover milk protein can make hair feel stiff. Use right away and wash out the same day.

name: Unsalted butter (dairy)
good: The base of traditional East African hair butters (kibe). Washed and whipped, it's a rich, softening fat for dry hair.
care: It's a food fat: it goes rancid and sour-smelling, faster if water is whipped in. Make small batches, keep them in the fridge, and wash out within a few hours.

name: Reishi mushroom (lingzhi), dried powder
good: A traditional East Asian tonic mushroom, added to K-beauty scalp products as an antioxidant.
care: No human evidence for hair or scalp. Low risk on skin; don't take it by mouth without asking a doctor if you're on blood thinners.

name: Woad leaf (Isatis, daqingye), dried
good: Traditional cooling herb; also the old source of indigo dye, so it tints a bar blue-green.
care: Lab studies only. Can stain light fabrics and very pale hair slightly.

name: Goji berry (black or red), dried
good: Antioxidant-rich berry used in East Asian hair tonics.
care: No evidence it does anything for hair in a wash-off product. Low risk.

name: Mulberry leaf or root bark, dried
good: Used in K-beauty for soothing and brightening; leaf powder colours bars green.
care: Lab and small studies only. Low risk.

name: Perfumer's alcohol (SDA 40-B, 190 to 200 proof)
good: Odourless, cosmetic-grade ethanol made undrinkable with a bittering agent. Dissolves fragrance oil into a clear spray that dries fast, and at this strength it preserves itself.
care: Very flammable: mix away from flames and stoves. Can dry or sting broken or freshly shaved skin. Not the same as rubbing (isopropyl) alcohol, which is never for perfume. Let a new blend rest 2 days to 2 weeks before using.

name: Calendula-infused oil (jojoba, olive or sunflower)
good: Carrier oil soaked with dried calendula petals. Gentle and soothing for dry, chapped skin.
care: Use fully dried petals so no water gets in. Skip if you're allergic to ragweed or daisies.

name: Sodium sulfate (Glauber's salt, bath grade)
good: The main salt in Japanese medicated bath powders and many hot springs. Dissolved in the tub it makes the water feel softer and the warmth seem to last longer.
care: For the bath only; never eat it. Use bath or cosmetic grade, about 25 to 30 g in a full tub. Not the same as sodium lauryl sulfate.

name: Trehalose
good: A gentle sugar humectant used in Japanese bath powders and skincare to hold water in the skin.
care: Low risk. Water-soluble; it can turn sticky in humid storage, so keep the jar closed.

name: Sodium lauryl sulfoacetate (SLSa)
good: A mild powdered foaming agent for bath bombs and soaks; also helps oils spread through the water instead of floating.
care: Fine powder: wear a mask while measuring. Not the same as SLS.

name: Sacha inchi seed oil
good: A light, omega-rich seed oil from Peru; softening and quick to absorb.
care: High in omega-3, so it goes rancid fast. Buy small, keep it cool, and add vitamin E.

name: Tamarind powder (dried pulp)
good: Dried tamarind pulp; contains tartaric acid, a mild fruit acid. The shelf-stable way to use tamarind in scrubs.
care: In a scrub that's rinsed off after a few minutes, the acid does little; the polish comes from the grains. Patch test.

name: Urea (cosmetic grade)
good: One of the best-studied moisturisers: 5 to 10% hydrates and softens; 10 to 20% smooths rough skin and KP.
care: Water-soluble, so it only works in creams, lotions or gels (needs a preservative). Can sting on cracked skin above 10%.

name: Manuka honey (UMF or MGO rated)
good: New Zealand honey with methylglyoxal (MGO), which gives it stronger antibacterial activity than ordinary honey. Medical-grade manuka dressings have real evidence for wounds and burns.
care: Kitchen manuka isn't sterile, so don't put it on open wounds; use a medical-grade dressing for that. For a face mask, any raw honey works almost as well; UMF 10+ or MGO 263+ is only worth paying for on blemishes.

name: Red bean (azuki) powder
good: Finely ground azuki beans; a traditional East Asian face and body wash powder that gently polishes and cleanses.
care: Grind very fine and sieve. Mix with water or yogurt only when you use it.

name: Rice bran powder (cám gạo, nuka)
good: The bran layer of rice; used for centuries in Japan and Vietnam as a gentle body polish. Softening and mildly exfoliating.
care: Goes rancid; buy small and keep it dry and cool.

name: Red sandalwood powder (rakta chandan)
good: Traditional Ayurvedic powder for ubtans and face packs; cooling, and gives a rosy colour.
care: Not the same tree as fragrant white sandalwood, and it has little scent. Can tint skin and towels pink-red briefly.

name: Lodhra bark powder (Symplocos)
good: Astringent Ayurvedic bark used in face packs for oily skin and blemishes.
care: Traditional use only; little research. Patch test.

name: Green gram flour (moong dal)
good: Gentle bean flour used in Indian ubtans as a mild cleanser and polish; softer than gram flour.
care: Grind fine and sieve. Mix with liquid only when you use it.

name: Chironji (charoli) seed powder
good: Rich, nutty seed ground with milk into a soft paste in traditional ubtans; adds oil and slip.
care: A nut-like seed: skip with tree nut allergies. Goes rancid; grind fresh.

name: Foaming whipped soap base (FSWB)
good: A ready-made, preserved whipped soap from soap suppliers; whips into a fluffy, foaming body wash or scrub base.
care: It's preserved, but adding water or a wet hand to the jar can still let mould in. Scoop with a dry spoon.

name: Poppy seeds
good: Tiny round seeds that add a gentle, rolling scrub and speckled look.
care: Can clog drains in large amounts; use a teaspoon or so.

name: Wars (ورس, Flemingia / kamala) powder
good: A saffron-yellow seed-pod powder from Yemen and East Africa, used in Gulf bridal and "brightening" body pastes for colour and a warm glow.
care: The glow is a temporary yellow tint, not lightening. Stains towels, nails and grout. Patch test; some people react.

name: Laurel (bay) soap, Aleppo-style (صابون الغار)
good: Traditional olive and laurel-berry oil soap from Syria. Gentle, real soap; grated and melted into Gulf "soap pastes".
care: Like all true soap it's alkaline and can dry; follow with moisturiser.

name: Tahini (sesame paste)
good: Rich, oily sesame paste that makes a mask creamy and softening.
care: Food: make fresh, rinse off. Skip with a sesame allergy.

name: Bitter almond oil (زيت اللوز المر)
flag: Use sweet almond, not bitter almond
good: A pressed oil sold in Middle Eastern shops for skin and hair.
care: Bitter almonds contain amygdalin, which releases cyanide; pressed oil is usually low in it but quality varies, and bitter almond essential oil is toxic unless labelled FFPA (prussic-acid-free). Sweet almond oil does the same job safely.

name: Mandelic acid
good: The gentlest AHA, from bitter almonds; smooths texture and helps uneven tone, often better tolerated on deeper skin.
care: Exfoliant: not on the same day as a scrub, retinoid or other acid. Sunscreen on exposed skin.

name: Jojoba beads (exfoliating)
